passage: Ganga's elbow caught the glass photo frame on the shelf, and it cracked across one corner. Her heart thudded. She turned the frame to face the wall, and when Charu came in from the kitchen and asked, "Did anyone touch the frame?" Ganga said, "Not me. Maybe the cat." Charu looked at the cat, then at Ganga, and spoke quietly, not loudly. "The glass could cut someone. I'm not angry about the frame. I need to know what happened so nobody gets hurt." Ganga's face went hot. "It was me. I didn't mean to." Charu put on slippers, swept up the pieces while Ganga watched from a safe distance, and wrapped the cracked frame in paper for the bin.

qa.q: What did Ganga blame at first?
qa.a: Ganga blamed the cat.

qa.q: Why did Ganga say "Not me"?
qa.a: Ganga was scared of being punished, and her heart thudded.

qa.q: What helped Ganga tell the truth?
qa.a: Charu stayed calm, said Charu was not angry about the frame, and explained that the glass could cut someone.

qa.q: How did Charu see the situation?
qa.a: Charu was mainly worried about safety, not about placing blame.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild who broke something and says it was not them, until a calm reaction makes the truth safe to tell.

passage:
"Alka, where's your maths test? Your teacher said it came back today."
"I... left it at school."
"Did you?"
"Yes. Probably."
"Alka, look at me. Is it in your bag?"
Silence. Alka's fingers tightened on the zip.
"Fourteen out of fifty," she whispered. "I thought you'd shout."
Santosh sat on the arm of the sofa. "I'm not happy about fourteen. But I'm happier you told me than if you'd hidden it. What went wrong?"
"I didn't understand fractions."
"Then we'll do ten minutes each evening. And you can show me marks straight away next time, even bad ones."

qa.q: What marks did Alka get?
qa.a: Alka got fourteen out of fifty.

qa.q: Why did Alka first say the test was left at school?
qa.a: Alka was afraid Santosh would shout and hoped to avoid that reaction.

qa.q: What could Alka do next time?
qa.a: Show the paper straight away and say what she did not understand.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about Alka's honesty?
qa.a: Santosh is unhappy about the marks but glad and relieved that Alka told the truth.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild hiding a poor test result out of fear of punishment until a calm reaction makes honesty possible.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4A, Tuesday.
At break, the flowerpot by our door was found broken. When I asked, Madhav said at once, "Not me, ma'am. It was already broken." He did not look at me. His ears were red. Divyansh had seen the ball hit it but said nothing.
I did not shout. Madhav has learned, from louder reactions before, to deny first. I told the class, "Pots break. I only want to know so we can clean it safely."
After lunch Madhav came to my table alone. "Ma'am, it was my ball." He was shaking.
I thanked him for telling me. We swept it up together, and he fetched a new pot from the school garden.
I will talk with his parents about responding calmly to mistakes.
— Class teacher

qa.q: What did Madhav say at once when asked?
qa.a: "Not me, ma'am. It was already broken."

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he denied it?
qa.a: Madhav was frightened of punishment; he did not look at the teacher and his ears were red.

qa.q: Which choice by the teacher helped Madhav tell the truth?
qa.a: Not shouting and saying pots break and the goal is to clean safely, which made it feel safe for Madhav to own up.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have felt watching this?
qa.a: Divyansh might have felt uneasy and torn, knowing the truth but not wanting to tell on a classmate in front of everyone.

grounding: Illustrates a child who denies breaking something out of fear of punishment, and a calm response that makes honesty feel safe.

passage:
Dear Diary,
We got our maths test back. I got 9 out of 25. I folded it very small and pushed it inside the torn lining of my school bag.
At dinner Ritu didi asked. I said, "Ma'am hasn't given it back yet." My heart was going so fast. Didi looked at me for a long time.
Last time I got a low mark, Papa shouted for half an hour and took away cricket for a month. So now I hide. I don't even feel bad about the lie. I feel bad about the 9.
But it needs a signature by Friday.
Tonight Didi sat on my bed. "Kamal, whatever it is, I'll sit with you when you tell Mummy." I nearly cried.
Maybe tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Kamal get on the maths test?
qa.a: I got 9 out of 25.

qa.q: Why did Kamal hide the test paper?
qa.a: Kamal was afraid of being shouted at and punished again, as after the last low mark.

qa.q: How could Kamal's parents help Kamal stop hiding things?
qa.a: They could respond calmly to low marks and help with the maths, so telling the truth no longer feels dangerous.

qa.q: How might Ritu didi feel sitting on the bed?
qa.a: Ritu didi seems worried and caring, sensing the lie and gently offering to sit with Kamal while telling Mummy.

grounding: Shows a child who hides a poor test paper and lies because a harsh reaction last time taught hiding, not improving.

passage:
Outside the flour mill in Sehore, Vinita's tyre rolled into Uday kaka's bicycle. The bicycle fell, and its bell cracked.
Uday kaka came out, white with flour and red with anger. "Who did this?"
Vinita hid the stick behind her back. "The goat, kaka. The goat pushed it."
Uday kaka looked at the goat, tied ten steps away, and shouted about children until people stopped to watch. Vinita said "goat" again, louder.
That evening her grandmother heard the story from a neighbour. She did not shout. She sat Vinita down with a glass of milk. "Was it the goat?"
Vinita looked at the glass. "No, Aaji." Her voice was very small.
"Then tomorrow we go to kaka together, and you tell him. I'll be right there."

qa.q: What cracked when the bicycle fell?
qa.a: Its bell cracked.

qa.q: Why did Vinita say "goat" again, louder?
qa.a: Vinita was frightened by Uday kaka's shouting and the crowd, so hiding felt safer than telling the truth.

qa.q: What did Aaji do that led Vinita to tell the truth?
qa.a: Aaji stayed calm, asked quietly and promised to stand beside Vinita, which made honesty feel safe.

qa.q: How might Uday kaka's shouting have made Vinita's lie stronger?
qa.a: The loud anger in front of people made Vinita more scared, so she held on to the lie instead of owning up.

grounding: Illustrates a child who blames a goat for breaking a bicycle bell out of fear, while shouting deepens the hiding and calm makes honesty possible.

passage:
During wet break in their Kraków classroom, Olga tossed a rubber ball to Thabo and it hit the globe on the teacher's desk. The globe rolled off, and a crack split right across the Atlantic.
Pan Nowak came back and stared at it. "Who did this?"
Olga's stomach went tight. Last month he had made Kuba stand in the corridor the whole afternoon for spilling paint. "It was already cracked," she said. "It was like that this morning."
Thabo looked at the floor and said nothing.
Pan Nowak frowned but moved on to spelling. Olga didn't hear a single word of the lesson. On the bus home, Thabo said quietly, "You didn't have to say that." Olga pressed her forehead against the cold window and didn't answer.

qa.q: What happened to the globe?
qa.a: It rolled off the desk and a crack split right across the Atlantic.

qa.q: Why did Olga say the globe was already cracked?
qa.a: Olga was scared of being punished, remembering that Pan Nowak made Kuba stand in the corridor all afternoon for spilling paint.

qa.q: What could make it easier for Olga to tell the truth next time?
qa.a: If Pan Nowak met accidents calmly, for example by asking who could help fix things rather than punishing, Olga might feel safe enough to own up.

qa.q: What is it like for Thabo when Olga blames the globe's crack on the morning?
qa.a: Thabo seems uncomfortable and torn, staring at the floor in class and later saying quietly, "You didn't have to say that."

grounding: Shows a schoolchild lying about a breakage out of fear of a harsh punishment seen earlier.
